cards.q: Which of these is not a valid IPv4 address?
cards.why: Each of the four numbers is one byte, 0 to 255; 256 does not fit.

cards.q: How many addresses can be given to devices in a /{p} subnet?
cards.why: 32 − p bits are left for the host: $2^{32-p}$ addresses, less the network and broadcast addresses.

cards.q: A device is 192.168.1.{h} with mask 255.255.255.{m}. What is the last number of its network address?
cards.why: Block size = 256 − the mask's last number; the network is the multiple of it at or just below the address.

cards.q: How does an Ethernet switch decide which port to send a frame out of?
options: By destination MAC, learned from past frames
By IP address, looked up in its routing table
It sends every frame out of every port
By the length and type of the frame
cards.why: A switch learns which MAC address is on which port from the frames that arrive, then forwards each frame only where it needs to go (flooding only unknown ones).

cards.q: What does a VLAN do?
options: Makes the switch forward frames faster
Encrypts all traffic between the ports
Lets two devices share one IP address
Splits one switch into separate networks
cards.why: A VLAN is a separate broadcast domain on the same hardware: machines on one VLAN cannot reach another without routing, which is where a firewall can sit.

cards.q: How long does it take to send {mb} MB over a {s} Mbit/s link, ignoring overheads, in seconds?
cards.why: Bytes to bits: × 8. Then ÷ the bit rate. Links are rated in bits; files in bytes.

cards.q: How does TCP differ from UDP?
options: UDP is always faster and more reliable than TCP
TCP has no port numbers at all, whereas UDP has them
TCP connects and resends lost data; UDP just sends
UDP is only ever used on the internet
cards.why: TCP gives an ordered, acknowledged stream; UDP sends single datagrams with no delivery promise, which suits streaming, discovery and some fieldbuses.

cards.q: Match each service with its usual TCP port.
cards.why: Well-known ports: a firewall rule names the port a service listens on.

cards.q: What identifies one TCP connection?
options: The IP address of the server alone
The IP address and port at each end
The MAC address of the client
The port number of the server alone
cards.why: Many clients can talk to port 502 on one PLC at once; each connection differs by the client's address and port.

cards.q: Which Wireshark display filter shows only Modbus TCP traffic?
options: tcp.port == 502
modbus = true
ip.port == 502
port 502 only
cards.why: Display filters name protocol fields: `tcp.port == 502`, or the dissector name `mbtcp`.

cards.q: Your laptop on a switch sees none of the traffic between a PLC and an HMI. Why?
options: Wireshark needs a paid licence to see any PLC traffic
PLCs always encrypt everything they send
The laptop's firewall blocks all capture
A switch only sends their frames to their ports
cards.why: A switch forwards frames only where they are addressed. Use a mirror (SPAN) port on a managed switch, or a network tap.

cards.q: A capture shows many TCP retransmissions and duplicate ACKs. What does that point to?
options: A wrong IP address set on one of the devices
The PLC has been switched into STOP mode
Frames being lost: cabling, duplex or overload
Nothing: every network shows plenty of these
cards.why: TCP resends what was not acknowledged. Lots of it means loss somewhere on the path; check port error counters and cables.

cards.q: Where do an RS-485 bus's terminating resistors go?
options: One at every device
One at each end of the bus
One at the master only
None: RS-485 needs no termination
cards.why: About 120 Ω at each end matches the cable, so signals do not reflect back. Terminating every node would load the bus down.

cards.q: How many masters can a Modbus RTU network have?
options: One
Two
One per slave
As many as there are devices
cards.why: One master (client) asks, and up to 247 addressed slaves (servers) answer in turn.

cards.q: A manual lists a value in holding register {reg:0}. Which zero-based address goes in the Modbus request?
cards.why: Registers 40001 onwards are numbered from 1 in manuals, but addressed from 0 on the wire: 40001 is address 0. The classic off-by-one.

cards.q: How do devices exchange data with MQTT?
options: Each device polls every other device directly
A master asks each of the slaves in turn
They all read and write one shared file
They publish to topics on a broker
cards.why: Publish and subscribe: publishers and subscribers never talk directly, only through the broker, which suits many devices and flaky links.

cards.q: What does OPC UA give that plain Modbus does not?
options: Faster scan times on serial links
Analogue values only, with no digital ones
Named, typed, browsable data, with security
A cheaper, thinner cable run to each device
cards.why: OPC UA carries an information model (nodes with names, types and units you can browse) and certificates and encryption. Modbus is numbered registers only.

cards.q: What does MQTT QoS 1 promise?
options: At most once: it may be lost
At least once, perhaps twice
Exactly once, never repeated
Delivered within one second
cards.why: QoS 0 at most once; QoS 1 at least once (duplicates possible, so the receiver must cope); QoS 2 exactly once, at more cost.

cards.q: How does EtherCAT move data?
options: One frame passes every slave, each using its part
Each slave in turn is sent its own separate frame by the master
Slaves send their data whenever it changes
Over a separate serial line to each slave
cards.why: Processing on the fly: the frame is read and written by each slave in passing and returns, so one frame serves the whole network each cycle.

cards.q: A motion bus updates each axis every {c} µs. An axis moves at {v} mm/s. How far does it move between updates, in µm?
cards.why: Distance = speed × time: mm/s × µs = nm, so ÷ 1000 for µm. A shorter cycle gives finer control.

cards.q: What are EtherCAT's distributed clocks for?
options: Timing out any frames that are lost
Setting the date and time on the HMI
Measuring the length of each cable
Keeping all slaves' clocks in step
cards.why: Synchronised clocks let every drive sample and apply its setpoint at the same moment, well under a microsecond apart: essential for coordinated motion.

cards.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: Back up three times a day, for two weeks, onto one external disk
Three PCs share two backups on one server
Three copies, on two kinds of media, one of them off site
Keep backups for three years, two months and one day
cards.why: Any single failure, theft or fire should still leave a copy.

cards.q: Why image a line PC's whole disk, not just copy its project files?
options: Project files alone cannot be copied off
Rebuilding Windows and its software takes days
An image is always smaller than the files
Disk images are required by law on site
cards.why: A disk image restores the whole working machine in an hour; the files alone leave you reinstalling everything around them.

cards.q: When is a backup proven?
options: When a test restore has worked
When the backup software says it succeeded
When the file is the right size
When it is stored off site
cards.why: Only a test restore shows the backup is complete and usable.

cards.q: In SCADA, what is a tag?
options: A printed label fixed to a cable or terminal
A user's name and password for the HMI
One screen of the operator HMI display
A named data point linked to a PLC address
cards.why: Tags are SCADA's variables: each one reads or writes a PLC address and carries its engineering units, limits and history settings.

cards.q: A historian logs {n} tags every {s} s, 8 bytes per value, uncompressed. How many MB is that per day?
cards.why: Values per day per tag = 86 400 ÷ {s}; × {n} tags × 8 bytes; ÷ 1 000 000 for MB.

cards.q: A redundant pair of SCADA servers runs as hot standby. What does that mean?
options: The standby is started by hand after a failure
Both servers write to the PLCs at the same time
The standby keeps in step and takes over by itself
The standby server only ever keeps backups
cards.why: Hot standby: the second server is running, with the same data, and takes over automatically. Cold standby needs someone to start it.

cards.q: What is the safest way to give a supplier remote access to a PLC?
options: Port-forward the PLC to the internet
A site-controlled VPN, on only when needed
A remote desktop tool left running
One password shared by all suppliers
cards.why: Access should be off by default, logged, per person (with multi-factor authentication) and through a point the site controls.

cards.q: In IEC 62443, what are zones and conduits?
options: Groups of assets, and the controlled links between them
Hazardous areas and the cable trays between them
Wi-Fi channels and the aerials that carry them
PLC racks and the backplanes that join them
cards.why: Divide the plant into zones, and allow only the traffic that must cross between them, through defined, filtered conduits.

cards.q: Why put a copy of the historian in a DMZ between the office and plant networks?
options: It makes the historian's queries run faster
The DMZ has more disk space than the plant
So suppliers can write straight to the PLCs
Office users read the copy, so nothing reaches in
cards.why: The plant pushes data out to the DMZ; the office reads it there. Nothing needs to connect inwards to the plant network.
